changes.before: How a drug-response dataset is split decides what a model's accuracy means: hold out cell lines to test personalised prediction, hold out drugs to test drug design, hold out tissues to test repurposing; holding out random pairs only tests imputation.
changes.after: A drug-response split tests prediction for withheld cell lines, drugs, tissues or pairs. Accuracy on that task does not by itself show clinical benefit or successful drug development.
changes.reason: Separate task-specific prediction from its proposed clinical or development application.

changes.before: Bernett and colleagues' DrEval framework evaluates drug-response prediction models under explicit protocols, holding out cell lines, drugs or tissues so that a model is scored on the generalisation it claims, and finds that many published gains shrink under the harder splits. Training on one screen and testing on another (cross-study validation) is the sternest bar because assays, cell-line panels and summary statistics differ. Random pair splits leak both the cell line and the drug into training and should only support imputation claims.
changes.after: A drug-response split defines which information is new when a model is evaluated. DrEval holds out cell lines, drugs, tissues or cell-line and drug pairs, with tuning performed separately inside the development data (Bernett and colleagues, 2026). The authors motivate these tasks by personalised prediction, drug design, repurposing and imputation, respectively. Those are intended applications: predicting a response in a held-out cell line or tissue does not establish benefit for a patient or successful repurposing. A random pair split can test a missing pair while its cell line and drug are represented in development; it does not test transfer to a new cell line or drug. Cross-study evaluation asks another question: whether predictions transfer between screens whose response measurements may differ. In DrEval's selected cross-study comparisons the molecular input profiles were shared, so even that evaluation did not test every change a future dataset might introduce. These splits answer different questions and have no universal order of difficulty.
changes.reason: Remove the unsupported universal sternest-bar hierarchy; retain the paper's task-to-application motivation with explicit boundaries.

changes.before: Drug sensitivity is how strongly a tumour or cell line is held back by a compound; it is summarised by the concentration that halves growth (IC50) or by the area under the whole dose-response curve.
changes.after: Drug sensitivity describes response in a specified assay. An IC50 is the concentration producing half-maximal inhibition of its measured endpoint; it does not always mean half the growth.
changes.reason: An assay endpoint is not necessarily growth or a growth-rate-normalised measure.

changes.before: The half maximal inhibitory concentration, IC50, measures the potency of a substance in inhibiting a biological function, the amount needed to inhibit a process by half in vitro (Wikipedia). Cell-line screens such as GDSC and CTRP report IC50, GI50 and the area under (or above) the dose-response curve for hundreds of drugs across hundreds of lines. The readouts are not interchangeable: different viability assays (CellTiter-Glo versus Syto60) and different summary statistics are a known source of disagreement between datasets.
changes.after: Drug-response measurements belong to a specified assay, exposure time, endpoint and analysis. An IC50 is a concentration associated with half-maximal inhibition of the endpoint defined for that assay; an area under a dose-response curve also depends on the concentration range and response scale. GDSC's 2013 resource paper describes fluorescence-based cell-viability measurements after 72 hours, with curves fitted across nine concentrations to derive IC50, slope and area under the curve (Yang and colleagues). That is a viability readout, rather than a direct count of cell divisions. Hafner and colleagues' 2016 study shows that conventional IC50, maximal effect and area-under-curve values can depend on how many divisions occur during an assay, and introduces growth-rate inhibition measures to address that dependence. A predicted assay IC50 is a model output, and is not a measured response, an equilibrium dissociation constant or evidence of treatment benefit in a patient. Cer and colleagues' 2009 IC50-to-Ki tool makes the biochemical distinction explicit: conversion depends on the interaction mechanism, concentrations and other assumptions.
changes.reason: Replace the growth-only shorthand and unverified cross-screen generalisation with the read papers' assay-specific definitions.

changes.before: Variant-effect prediction estimates a specified consequence of a sequence change, whereas variant calling identifies changes from sequence data. Ensembl maps each allele of a variant onto every overlapping transcript with a rule-based approach, so the same genomic change can have a different consequence in different transcripts, and its impact categories (high, moderate, low, modifier) are qualitative assumptions about likely effect, not a measured loss of function (Ensembl documentation, release 116). A score from a missense tool does not answer a splice or regulatory question, and a prediction should name the reference genome, the alleles and the transcript (with its version) it was made for. A raw model score is not automatically a probability: a splice score of 0.92 on an unspecified scale does not mean a 92 per cent chance of lost function, because thresholds and evidence strengths belong to a particular tool and task. The absence of a prediction does not make a variant benign, because a tool may not cover that variant type or transcript. RNA junction evidence, functional experiments and clinical studies address different gaps, and none is interchangeable with a sequence score. Two reports of the same prediction from the same software version are two copies of one computed result, not two independent experiments. Where a tool's training data overlap the variants used to evaluate it, its performance can be overestimated, which is why the ClinGen calibration of thirteen missense tools to ACMG/AMP pathogenicity and benignity evidence strengths, estimated from local positive predictive value, used datasets assembled to minimise that circularity (Pejaver and colleagues, 2022). That calibration used ClinVar missense variants classified as pathogenic or benign and rare in gnomAD, within the ACMG/AMP recommendations for variants in genes associated with monogenic disease, and it selected no tool designed for splice variants. Its introduction notes that many methods overlap and so do not offer independent assessment of pathogenicity, which is why agreement between tools that share training data or inputs is not independent confirmation. The AMP, ASCO and CAP guideline for somatic variants notes that early prediction algorithms were developed and validated for germline variants and recommends that their results never be used as the sole evidence for variant classification or clinical decision making (Li and colleagues, 2017).

before: Assay distinction. A predicted binding IC50 estimates a competitive-binding assay endpoint. An IC50 depends on the assay conditions and is not automatically an equilibrium dissociation constant. Cer and colleagues' 2009 IC50-to-Ki tool calculates binding or inhibition constants using the interaction mechanism, concentrations and other assumptions; this is a biochemical distinction, not validation of an HLA model or a measure of cancer-cell growth inhibition. Reading guide (OnCo inference): Record the model and version, allele, peptide length, prediction task, units, reference distribution and threshold beside every score, and do not put a rank and an IC50 in one unlabelled column. A threshold is a selection rule for a stated workflow and cannot repair the wrong allele or an unsupported task. Inputs are peptide or source-protein sequences and an exact allele; scoring uses no tumour tissue; held-out validation, allele coverage and the endpoint (binding, recovery or T-cell recognition) decide what a good score means.
